Rule: Single-column, reverse-chronological, education and research before employment for a master's applicant
Source (tier): Both runs: Princeton/Cornell/UPenn/Harvard GSAS/UToronto (university career+admissions guidance)

Rule: Body text 11pt target, 10-12pt range; consistent throughout. (Runs quote Oxford differently: '11pt minimum' vs '10 or 11pt' -- 11 satisfies both readings.)
Source (tier): Both runs: Oxford Careers; Warwick; Harvard GSAS; Princeton

Rule: Margins equal on all four sides, 0.75-1.0 inch (19-25mm)
Source (tier): Both runs: UPenn; Texas Tech; CU Boulder

Rule: Standard system faces only (Times New Roman, Arial, Calibri, Cambria, Garamond, Georgia, Helvetica, Verdana); serif-vs-sans is designer's taste -- both runs independently confirm no admissions-side rule exists AMENDED 2026-09-12: the list above is Word-centric and omits DejaVu Sans, which is what this platform actually renders in -- the web image ships fonts-dejavu-core and no Helvetica. Changing the production face at all changes text metrics, hence page count, hence a BINDING max_pages constraint.

Rule: Applicant name is the largest element: 14-18pt (runs give 16-18 and 14-18), bold, top of page; contact plain below
Source (tier): Both runs: Texas Tech; TAMU; RISD; UW

Rule: Section headers left-aligned, bold, CAPS/small-caps, applied consistently; a thin bottom rule is an accepted delineator; never underline text for emphasis
Source (tier): Both runs: Princeton; Harvard GSAS; WVU

Rule: Non-DACH default: institution/role/degree flush LEFT, dates pushed RIGHT -- 'what' over 'when'
Source (tier): Both runs: Oxford Careers; UPenn; Harvard GSAS; McMaster

Rule: DACH tabellarischer Lebenslauf is a strict two-column grid: dates/labels in the LEFT column, descriptions right, precise vertical alignment, reverse-chronological now accepted. Advisory by default; some programmes state it (verify per programme before loading as BINDING)

Source (tier): Both runs agree on the layout; Gemini claims LMU/Heidelberg request it (programme pages, unverified); layout detail from commercial guides
Source URL [provenance]: https://leelink.de/german-cv/ [commercial; layout corroborated by both runs]

Rule: Length when uncapped: 1-2 FULL pages for a master's application (fill the last page or cut to the previous one); the uncapped 'academic ledger' CV applies to research-track cases where the programme invites a full CV
Source (tier): Runs disagree (Claude: 1-2 full, Oxford admissions; Gemini: uncapped, UToronto/Harvard) -- resolved for the master's-admissions audience

Rule: Bullet points for experience entries (active verbs, no pronouns); a short prose block is acceptable for research/thesis entries where the reader is a specialist
Source (tier): Both runs; the research-entry nuance is Claude-run only

Rule: Publications: one citation style flawlessly consistent, applicant's own name bolded, author order preserved, DOI as resolvable link, published works strictly separated from in-preparation/under-review
Source (tier): Both runs: CU Boulder; UToronto; U Sydney; Oxford

Rule: Most master's applicants have no publications and tutors do not expect them; the section is conditional, never padded
Source (tier): Claude run: Mastersportal; The Job Studio

Rule: ORCID (and Scholar/GitHub/personal site where relevant) in the contact header; hyperlinks live in the PDF. AMENDED 2026-08-30: the original clause 'URL text readable, not buried in anchor text' is CONTRADICTED by the accessibility standards, which say the opposite -- never use a URL as link text, because a screen-reader user tabbing through links in isolation gets a protocol and a path rather than a destination. Use a labelled handle ('GitHub: 0rkhann'). The print argument behind the original clause is real -- a paper or link-stripped copy loses the address -- and is the reason to keep ORCID's identifier as its own text, where the identifier IS the destination. It is not the stronger argument in general.
Source (tier): AMENDED against Section508.gov, WCAG.com, Yale Usability, UC Office of the President, Level Access; original was U Sydney + BU/IU helpsheets
Source URL [provenance]: https://www.section508.gov/blog/accessibility-bytes/descriptive-links-and-hypertext [US federal accessibility standard]; https://usability.yale.edu/digital-accessibility/accessibility-resources/accessibility-articles/accessible-links [university]; https://researcher-hub.sydney.edu.au/career-development/cv-writing/academic-cv-tips-and-tricks.html [original, now the minority view]
Confidence: High (amended); the superseded clause was High on one source only

Rule: Languages: plain text list, CEFR code (optionally + plain word), recent test score adjacent; never bars, dots, stars or percentages. RECHECKED 2026-08-30 and upheld against a proposal to use the Europass self-assessment grid on every variant: that grid is the official EUROPASS layout specifically, and table structures are what CV parsers most reliably scramble. The 'optionally + plain word' clause is the answer to a sparse-looking section
Source (tier): Both runs: Council of Europe; Cambridge; Turkish academic pages

Rule: No photos (in no-photo destinations), icons, infographics, color blocks, skill graphics, or decorative two-column templates; typographic hierarchy through weight and space only
Source (tier): Both runs: RISD; academic-CV guidance; Turkish YOK guidance

Rule: Left-justify body text; do not center critical information
Source (tier): Gemini run: WVU; consistent with Claude run's layout reference

Source (tier): Runs disagree on strength (Claude: 1 page via commercial; Gemini: gap via Sorbonne/U-Paris absence)

Rule: Netherlands/Nordics: no published visual norms; clean minimalist default, 1-2 pages preferring shorter, no overselling
Source (tier): Both runs: Leiden/Utrecht/UvA (NL, university); Nordic evidence commercial-only

Rule: UK/Ireland watch item: UKRI/Royal Society R4RI 'narrative CV' (four prose modules, no bullets) is becoming standard for research FUNDING applications; not a master's-admissions default -- revisit if the catalog adds a scheme that requires it

Source (tier): Gemini run: UKRI; Royal Society

Rule: Reviewers cull on carelessness: typos, mixed styles, inconsistent alignment, cramped leading, widowed pages (a near-empty final page reads as careless)
Source (tier): Both runs: GoGrad; career services; academic-editing literature

Rule: Name + page number on each page of a multi-page CV
Source (tier): Claude run only: TAMU/UW/UCSB

Rule: Reader conditions: bulk skimming, left-loaded scanning, cognitive ease rewarded. ALL timing figures are contaminated (US-undergraduate CBE data; the '6-second scan' is an employment study both runs were told to exclude and one cited anyway) -- take the design implication (skimmable, left-loaded, legible), never the numbers
Source (tier): Claude run: Chronicle/IHE (undergrad, labeled); Gemini run: TheLadders/resumefast (employment, ground-rule violation, flagged at merge)

Rule: Skills section is optional and secondary on an academic CV; when present, restrict it to technical and research-specific competencies (languages, software, laboratory/computational techniques) with proficiency indicated. Transferable skills (writing, collaboration, analysis) belong in the experience bullets that evidence them, not in an asserted list
Source (tier): Berkeley Career Engagement academic-CV guide carries no skills section at all, only Languages and Professional Training; Bath Careers (master's applications); Columbia GSAS

Rule: Every experience or research bullet answers three questions in one or two lines: what was done, how (method or tool), and with what result -- quantified where a number exists. Oxford teaches the CAR mnemonic (Challenge, Action, Result); the outcome-first XYZ variant ('accomplished X as measured by Y by doing Z') is the same content reordered. One idea per bullet, strong specific opening verb, 5-6 bullets per role at most, and never open with 'Responsible for' or 'Worked on'
Source (tier): Oxford Careers (CAR); SJSU Career Center (verb+task+method+result)

Rule: Grade is stated on the institution's OWN scale, mark and denominator together ('16.45/20.0', '3.82/4.0', '8.7/10.0') -- never converted silently -- with the honours classification alongside it where one was awarded. For graduate applications the grade is expected rather than optional. SEARCHED AND NOT FOUND: no source states the number of semesters a grade covers, or a period alongside it; the degree's own date range already carries that. Do not add it
Source (tier): Convergent CV guides; the negative is a documented search result

Rule: An experience entry names WHERE as precisely as the reader needs: an academic post names the group or laboratory and its principal investigator, an industry post names the company. Both carry a month-year range. An entry missing its employer, its supervisor (academic) or its dates is incomplete, not merely brief
Source (tier): Oxford (name supervisors); Arizona/UPenn section guidance (organisation, title, dates)

Rule: Discipline-switch applicant (e.g. a petroleum or chemical engineering bachelor's applying to a master's in AI): the degree title is stated honestly and never reworded, and the ADJUSTMENT is in the supporting detail -- relevant coursework under the degree, projects and methods promoted above unrelated employment, and a technical skills section placed early. Relevant modules are worth listing precisely when experience in the target field is thin, which is the switcher's case
Source (tier): Convergent CV guidance on tailoring the education section; module-listing guidance for applicants with limited direct experience
Confidence: Medium -- commercial sources only; no university careers page found stating it directly

Rule: Conference presentations and posters are their OWN section, separate from publications. Merging them either inflates the publication record or hides the presentations; both are failures of the same separation S-011 draws between published and unpublished work
Source (tier): Arizona ('CONFERENCES / TALKS'); Wordvice/UPenn section lists

Rule: Contact details belong in the document BODY, never in a PDF page header or footer: resume parsers routinely skip header/footer regions, so a name and address placed there are invisible to the system even though a human sees them. (tehsil: cv_base.html's .contact-header is a flex row in the body flow, not a page header, so the standard variant already complies. The per-page 'Name - n/N' running head carries no unique information and is therefore not at risk.)
Source (tier): SCU Career Center (university careers service); quickcv 8-system parser test (vendor test, method stated); remaining corroboration is vendor content marketing
Confidence: Medium (consistent across sources; sourcing tier weak)

Rule: Content that must survive MACHINE PARSING goes in a single-column flow; multi-column layouts and tables are the most frequently reported parsing failure, because parsers read left-to-right line-by-line and merge the columns into one scrambled string. SCOPE, AND WHY THIS DOES NOT CONFLICT WITH S-008 (resolved 2026-09-12): every source found for this rule describes CORPORATE job-application ATS (Workday, Greenhouse, iCIMS, Taleo, Lever). A targeted search for evidence that GRADUATE ADMISSIONS portals parse an uploaded CV returned nothing -- no admissions system, only job-ATS material. Absence of evidence, so treat it as unproven rather than disproven. Independently, tehsil's own pipeline hands no CV to a parser: the only exit for a rendered document is storage.py's download (Content-Disposition: attachment, read by a human), and portal automation TYPES verified values into form fields -- session.py's FILL_METHODS allows only fill, type, selectOption and selectOptionFromDropdown, so there is no file-upload action for a parser to receive. So S-008's two-column DACH grid, the Europass table and the SISGP template are NOT in violation, and the two layouts mandated by their destination (Europass, SISGP/R-079) could not yield to this rule anyway. S-008 is the only one where a choice exists, and it keeps its table. WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS LIVE: a destination shown to parse an uploaded CV, or a portal step that uploads a file rather than typing fields. The answer then is a per-destination variant -- format_resolution.py already selects a variant from what the programme requires -- never a weakening of S-008 or a single 'safe' layout for every destination.
Scope: job-application ATS; unproven for graduate admissions
Source (tier): quickcv 8-system parser test: two-column failed in 7 of 8 (vendor test, method stated); SCU Career Center; UPenn Career Services (job resumes, not admissions). Admissions-portal parsing: searched 2026-09-12, no evidence found either way. Scope resolution: tehsil code (apps/documents/storage.py, apps/portals/session.py::FILL_METHODS)
Confidence: Medium for the parsing claim itself (one method-stating vendor test, one university careers service); High that it does not bind tehsil today (verified in code, 2026-09-12)

Rule: Dates as 'Month Year', written or abbreviated ('Sep 2020 - Jun 2024'). The 8-system test parsed that form correctly everywhere; numeric-only formats errored in 3 systems and year-only ranges made 4 flag a finished position as current or undated, one of which then computed a false employment gap from it. (tehsil: the month_year filter already renders exactly this form in every variant, so this rule records a property to keep, not a change to make.)
Source (tier): quickcv 8-system parser test (vendor test, method stated); SCU Career Center ('MM/YYYY or Month Year, consistently')
Confidence: Medium (single test, but it reports per-system results)

Rule: Experience entry header: THREE layouts are attested and the choice is the house's, not a rule. Measured in ONE document -- University of Toronto's 'Creating your academic CV for Masters and PhDs' -- sample 1 prints role bold on line 1 with the dates right and the employer + city on line 2; sample 3 prints teaching roles as one line 'Title, Course, Institution, Term'; sample 2 puts the dates in a left column. Oxford states the binding part: 'We would recommend writing your role/position and the name of the organisation on the left-hand side of the page and the dates on the right-hand side', and its CAR note adds 'Context: the organisation name, your job title and dates is often sufficient'. So what is fixed is role+organisation LEFT and dates RIGHT (S-007); how many lines they occupy is free. (tehsil: _cv_experience.html's two-line form is sample 1 exactly -- it needs no change. What DOES break the layout is a title field carrying a project name, which wraps the bold line and pushes the employer out of the scan path; ExperienceEntry has no project/thesis field, so an extractor puts it in `title`.)
Source (tier): University of Toronto Student Life (graduate CV guide, four worked samples); Oxford University Careers Service
Source URL [provenance]: https://www.studentlife.utoronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/Creating-Your-Academic-CV.pdf [university careers service, worked samples]; https://www.careers.ox.ac.uk/cvs [university careers service]

Rule: Awards section: the BULLET MARKER is a free choice, the AWARDING BODY is not. Same Toronto guide, three samples, three markers -- sample 1 unmarked ('Instructor of the Year, 2019, 2020' over 'Doctor of Pharmacy program, University of Toronto'), sample 2 unmarked with the money value in a left column, sample 4 bulleted ('- NSERC Postgraduate Scholarship B ... , 2019'). No source found prescribes either. What EVERY sample carries is the granting faculty or institution beside the award name, plus Toronto's own instruction that an unfamiliar award may take 'a brief line below the honour or award name that explains what the award is for or its primary criteria', and UPenn's 'Commonly known honors (Phi Beta Kappa) need no explanation, but other awards can be briefly explained'. Oxford goes further and nests awards under the education entry that earned them rather than in a section of their own. AMENDED 2026-09-15 against University College Cork, which is the most specific source found: "State funding body, terms, duration and amount" (its own example, "IRCSS funded fees and EUR 12,000 stipend"); where the reader will not know the award, "indicate the level of competition" ("one of six recipients selected from 3000 applicants"); "include any prestigious award offered but not taken up"; and "Mention any application that is currently under consideration". (tehsil: AwardEntry was title + date ONLY. awarding_body and detail ADDED 2026-09-15 -- one prose `detail` rather than four typed fields, because UCC's own example is a sentence and typed fields invite a model to compose one instead of copying the document's. The two STATUS cases UCC names -- an award declined, an application pending -- are deliberately NOT modelled: both are claims about something that did not happen, and this ledger verifies claims against a document. This also settles the separate question of a FUNDING/GRANTS heading: UCC keeps one and UQ calls its heading 'Research grants and relevant awards', but for a master's applicant two or three items do not justify splitting the section once the entry carries a body and an amount. Fix the model, not the section list.)
Source (tier): University of Toronto Student Life (graduate CV guide, three worked samples); UPenn Career Services; Oxford University Careers Service; UC Berkeley Career Engagement

Rule: Section inventory: FOUR headings recur across non-US and US guidance that tehsil's CVContent cannot hold at all. (a) PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT / TRAINING / CERTIFICATIONS -- 'all courses, workshops, certifications, and field specific tutorials or qualifying programs' (Toronto), 'Professional development activities' (Queensland), 'Professional Training' (Berkeley), 'Zertifikate und Weiterbildungen' (DE). (b) PROFESSIONAL AFFILIATIONS AND MEMBERSHIPS (Toronto, Queensland, Berkeley, UPenn). (c) VOLUNTARY / COMMUNITY / EXTRACURRICULAR ACTIVITY -- Oxford makes it a named third section ('INTERESTS or COMMUNITY ACTIVITY AND SKILLS'), Utrecht lists 'extra-curricular activities and interests', German guidance treats 'Ehrenamt und Engagement' as carrying real weight for a university application, and SISGP MANDATES it as a heading ('NETWORK-CIVIL SOCIETY ENGAGEMENT', R-064). (d) PROJECTS -- already named by R-026's own taught-track order ('Education -> Experience -> Projects -> Skills -> Languages -> Awards') and never built. Also recurrent but arguably already covered: research grants and fellowships as their own heading, separate from prizes (Queensland: 'Research grants and relevant awards'); teaching experience as its own heading rather than inside Experience (Toronto, UPenn, Berkeley). (tehsil: CVContent holds education, experience, research, publications, awards, skills, languages, references, summary. ExperienceEntry.unpaid exists but ONLY the Rhodes variant reads it, so voluntary work renders identically to a paid job everywhere else. Adding a heading is a schema change plus a ledger-extraction change, not a template change -- nothing in the pipeline collects a certificate or a membership today.)
Source (tier): University of Toronto Student Life; University of Queensland Graduate Research School; Oxford University Careers Service; Utrecht University; UC Berkeley Career Engagement; UPenn Career Services; German student-CV guidance (commercial, corroborating only)
Confidence: High (that the headings recur) / not yet decided (which ones tehsil adopts)

Rule: What goes INSIDE an entry, as opposed to how its lines are arranged (S-034). Two worked non-US guides agree field by field. (a) THESIS: printed under EDUCATION, attached to the degree, on its own labelled line -- Toronto sample 4 'Dissertation: Cognitive Models and Environmental Interface Designs'; UCC 'Thesis: "The physiognomy and facial expression of female characters..."'. It is never the title of an experience entry. A PROJECT carried out during a post is likewise not the post's title: Toronto's research sample keeps the role bare ('Research Assistant') and states the work in the first bullet. (b) FELLOWSHIP / FUNDING: named TWICE. Once inside the education entry it paid for -- UCC's worked example prints 'Funded by the Irish Research Council for Humanities and Social Sciences' as a line of the degree -- and once in Awards, where UCC requires 'State funding body, terms, duration and amount' (e.g. 'IRCSS funded fees and EUR 12,000 stipend') plus the level of competition where the award is unfamiliar ('one of six recipients selected from 3000 applicants'). A fellowship is never a job title. (c) ROLE TITLE: always present, always the bold left-hand element (Oxford; every sample in both guides). (d) INSTITUTION GRANULARITY differs by section. In EDUCATION the institution may stand alone on its row -- UCC does exactly that, institution left and dates right, with 'Include the qualifications under the relevant institutions'. In EXPERIENCE it may NOT: Toronto prints 'Department of Industrial Engineering, University of Toronto, 2018-2020' and 'Mount Sinai Hospital, Toronto, ON', and S-028 requires an academic post to name the group or laboratory. A bare 'EPFL' or 'University of Strasbourg' on an experience entry is under-specified. (e) SUPERVISOR: named, on a labelled line, as courtesy title + GIVEN NAME + SURNAME -- 'Supervisor: Dr. Carine Mendelsson' (Toronto), 'Supervisor: Dr. Cynthia Conway' (UCC). Both guides attach it to the degree AND, for research posts, Toronto folds it into a bullet instead ('under the supervision of Dr. C.M.Simon'). Initials are attested only in the bullet form. (tehsil: 'Thesis:' under education and 'Supervisor: <full name>' both already render correctly. ExperienceEntry.project ADDED 2026-09-15 -- before it an extractor put the project into `title`, which is what produced 'Research Intern, Project Title: Generative AI for peptide organocatalyst design' as a bold two-line header with 'EPFL' orphaned below it; the project is now its own italic line under the bare role and the supervisor shares the employer's line. THAT ARRANGEMENT IS A HOUSE CHOICE, NOT A SOURCED ONE: line 1 (role bold left, dates right) is Oxford and Toronto sample 1; a course or work title on its own line is Berkeley's teaching example; the supervisor named is Oxford / S-028. No source prints 'Employer -- Supervisor: Name' on one line, and Toronto's research sample instead keeps the role bare, prints 'Department, University, dates' beneath it, and names the supervisor inside the first bullet -- which this pipeline cannot do, because bullets are carried verbatim (S-010) and a project name folded into one is a reworded claim. STILL MISSING: a lab/group field on ExperienceEntry, a funding line on EducationEntry, and funding body / amount / duration / competition gloss on AwardEntry.)
Source (tier): University of Toronto Student Life (graduate CV guide, four worked samples); University College Cork Careers Service (PhD/postdoc CV guide, worked example); Oxford University Careers Service
Source URL [provenance]: https://www.studentlife.utoronto.ca/wp-content/uploads/Creating-Your-Academic-CV.pdf [university careers service, worked samples]; https://www.ucc.ie/en/media/support/careers/CVGuideforPhDandPostdoctoralResearchers.pdf [university careers service, worked example]; https://www.careers.ox.ac.uk/cvs [university careers service]

Rule: Project title and location on an experience entry: BOTH are attested, and one is BINDING somewhere in this catalog. (a) PROJECT TITLE -- yes for a research post, on its own labelled line. University College Cork's worked CV prints every research entry as institution+location / role / 'Project: "<title>" - Funded by <body>' / 'Supervisor: <name>' / bullets, three times over. Newcastle's workbook asks the education entry to 'Describe aims, methodology and achievements of your project'. The dissenting shape is CU Boulder, which gives an entry only 'date range, organization, title ... and a brief narrative' and lets the project live inside the narrative -- so the project is always NAMED, and only its placement varies. Nothing found argues for omitting the project ENTIRELY -- but resume-side guidance does argue against giving it a STANDALONE LINE, on the grounds that the bullets already say what the work was, and Arizona offers a third shape again: "Consider using a project title and/or name of the course IN PLACE OF a position title." OWNER DECISION 2026-09-15: no standalone project line. The field is still extracted, still in the ledger and still an include target; it is simply not printed. MEASURED BEFORE TAKING IT, on the CV it was decided against, counting each project title's content words that appear nowhere in that entry's own bullets: Groningen 0 of 7 lost (the line was pure repetition), EPFL 2 of 5 ('organocatalyst', 'design'), Master's Thesis 3 of 7 (including AZIMUTH, the thesis's actual name, which appears nowhere else on the document), ICIQ 5 of 5. So 'the bullets naturally take over' held on ONE entry in four; on the other three the information left the document. It could not be otherwise on this platform: bullets are carried verbatim from the ledger (S-010, and generation's prompt forbids merging, splitting or rewording them), so a bullet can only 'take over' if the applicant had already written the project into it. TWO CONSEQUENCES TO KNOW BEFORE RESTORING IT OR LEAVING IT OFF. (a) R-061 is BINDING and asks Europubhealth+ applicants for "full names of institutions, universities, projects" per experience; that programme renders through the same partial, and there is no per-programme switch for a FIELD -- cv_directives carry order and emphasise, not include -- so it is off for that destination too until one exists. (b) A thesis has a second, sourced home that this does not touch: S-037(a) puts it under the degree in EDUCATION as a labelled line, which is where AZIMUTH belongs and where the reader of a master's CV looks for it. (b) CITY AND COUNTRY -- yes, city + country, never a street address. Newcastle states the entry shape outright: 'Dates worked, job title, organisation, location (no need for full address)'. UCC's sample carries it in every entry, including the home institution ('Dept. of Genetics, University College Cork, Ireland'; 'Murdoch Children's Research Institute (MCRI), Sydney, Australia'). Queensland requires 'the name of the employing organisation, the city, and country'. Toronto's sample 1 prints 'Mount Sinai Hospital, Toronto, ON' -- though its own research sample omits the city, so Toronto is inconsistent with itself. CU Boulder requires neither. AND IT IS BINDING FOR AT LEAST ONE PROGRAMME: R-061, Europubhealth+, 'per experience, city + country; no abbreviations - full names of institutions, universities, projects' -- that one clause makes both halves of this rule mandatory at once. R-065 (Australia Awards) separately requires a 'duty station' column. (tehsil: ExperienceEntry.city/.country exist and render; they are EMPTY on real output because a real CV names the employer but not the town for four roles in five, and ingestion is rightly forbidden to supply one it knows from world knowledge. The only lawful source is the student, so the fix is a gap question, not a better prompt -- experience.project/.city/.country were added to constraints._INCLUDE_TARGETS 2026-09-15 so gaps.programme_required can ask. Before that, R-061 was unenforceable: no directive could carry it and nothing flagged the omission.)
Binding or advisory: advisory; BINDING where a programme states it (R-061, R-065)
Source (tier): University College Cork Careers Service (PhD/postdoc CV guide, worked example); Newcastle University Careers Service (academic CV workbook); University of Queensland Graduate Research School; University of Toronto Student Life; CU Boulder Career Services (the dissent); Europubhealth+ and Australia Awards programme instructions (binding)
Source URL [provenance]: https://www.ucc.ie/en/media/support/careers/CVGuideforPhDandPostdoctoralResearchers.pdf [university careers service, worked example]; https://www.ncl.ac.uk/mediav8/careers/documents/Academic%20CV%20workbook.pdf [university careers service]; https://cdf.graduate-school.uq.edu.au/academic-cv-guidelines [university graduate school]; https://www.colorado.edu/career/graduate-students/careers-academia/careers-academia-cv [university, dissenting]; https://www.europubhealth.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Instruction-2026-28_final-version-PDF.pdf [programme instructions, binding]

Rule: READ THIS BEFORE ADDING A SECTION: almost every published section inventory is FACULTY-CV inventory, and this platform's applicant is applying to a MASTER'S. University College Cork's guide is for "PhD and Postdoctoral Researchers"; Newcastle's workbook, Queensland's guidelines, Berkeley's and UPenn's lists and jobs.ac.uk's template are all written for an academic job search. Toronto's is the only one whose cover says "for Masters and PhDs". The two sources actually addressed to this audience are far shorter: OXFORD gives a graduate applicant THREE headings -- Education (with awards nested under the degree that earned them), Experience ("rather than 'Employment'", explicitly including voluntary work and student-society roles), and Interests or Community Activity and Skills -- and UTRECHT six: "education and qualifications, work experience, extra-curricular activities and interests, additional information, skills and referees". Against S-009 (1-2 FULL pages) the arithmetic settles it: the union of the faculty guides is around eighteen headings, and a master's applicant cannot fill eighteen without padding, which S-022 says reviewers cull on. So the answer to "the internet shows more sections" is TWO, not seven. Ranked, with the rejections and their reasons: (1) VOLUNTARY/COMMUNITY/CIVIL-SOCIETY -- Oxford makes it one of three, Utrecht lists it, German guidance weights Ehrenamt heavily for a university application, and SISGP MANDATES the heading (R-064, 'NETWORK-CIVIL SOCIETY ENGAGEMENT', where altering the category set 'will render your application ineligible'); ExperienceEntry.unpaid already exists and ONLY cv_funder_rhodes.html reads it, so this is a render-and-order change over an existing field. (2) PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT / CERTIFICATES / TRAINING -- Queensland, Toronto, Berkeley and German guidance; needs a new model and a new VerifiedFact category, so it is real work; the tell that it is missing is that the applicant's own CV filed 'Participation in summer school at the University of Strasbourg' under Awards. REJECTED: Projects (R-026 names it in our own taught-track order, but ResearchEntry plus ExperienceEntry.project now cover it -- amend R-026 instead); Professional memberships (every source for it is writing for a faculty job search, and a heading with one student-society line under it reads as padding); Teaching as its own heading (a split of Experience, worth doing only for a real teaching load); Research interests (overlaps `summary`, and R-085 routes motivation to the statement of purpose); Grants/Funding as its own heading (collapses into Awards -- see S-035).
Source (tier): Oxford University Careers Service and Utrecht University (the master's-audience sources); University College Cork, Newcastle, Queensland, Berkeley, UPenn, jobs.ac.uk (the faculty-audience sources this rule exists to discount); University of Toronto (both audiences)

Rule: What an EDUCATION entry carries, beyond the degree and the institution. University College Cork states the list: "Include dates, qualification, SUPERVISOR, dissertation, papers and awards", and its worked CV prints a funded degree's funder as a line of the degree -- "Funded by the Irish Research Council for Humanities and Social Sciences". Toronto's sample 4 prints the same pair under the degree, each labelled: 'Dissertation: Cognitive Models and Environmental Interface Designs' then 'Supervisor: Dr. Carine Mendelsson'. UCC adds that international students should INTERPRET a grade -- "indicate range of scores and size of class" -- which is what grade_conversion and class_rank already carry, and that it is typical to omit second-level qualifications. Relevant coursework belongs here too, by this catalog's own R-028 ("little research output: add research-relevant coursework") and S-029 (the discipline switcher states the degree title honestly and puts the adjustment in the supporting detail). The labels are load-bearing on THIS section, unlike the experience entry's project line (S-037): a bare name under an MSc says nothing about what that person did. (tehsil: supervisor, funding and relevant_coursework ADDED 2026-09-15 -- before them the thesis printed with no way to name who supervised it, R-028 had been in the catalog since the first research pass with no field able to satisfy it, and a funded degree lost its funder. Expected graduation date, which R-040 and R-016 want, needs no field: a future end_date already renders.)

Rule: An entry may exist ONLY to account for a gap, and then it carries no detail at all. University College Cork, on non-graduate and irrelevant roles: "Include name of organization and dates only to account for a possible gap (1 year +). Don't provide detail on irrelevant roles." Oxford says the same from the other side -- leave the reader wanting to learn more, do not include every last detail. This is not a style preference on this platform: R-042 requires gaps to be accounted for including mandatory military service, R-011 has DAAD PRIME requiring a CV with no chronological gaps, and R-020 notes universities requiring a gap-free CV from first school. (tehsil: NOT SATISFIED, and it is a schema constraint rather than an oversight. ExperienceEntry.bullets is `Field(min_length=1, max_length=12)`, so an entry with no bullets cannot be constructed and a legitimate gap-filler cannot be represented -- an applicant with an 18-month gap either invents a bullet or leaves the gap. Relaxing the minimum to 0 is a one-character change that removes S-010's only MECHANICAL enforcement, since every other style rule in this catalog is prose in a CSV; so this is a decision to take deliberately, not a cleanup. The narrower alternative is a typed `gap_filler` flag that waives the minimum for exactly this case and renders organisation and dates alone.)

Rule:
NEITHER the voluntary/community section NOR the certificates section is country-dependent. Searched 2026-09-15 and NOT FOUND: any country whose admissions guidance excludes voluntary work, community activity or extracurriculars from a CV. It is named positively in every destination checked -- UK (Oxford makes 'INTERESTS or COMMUNITY ACTIVITY AND SKILLS' one of only three headings it gives a graduate applicant, and puts 'voluntary work, student society roles' inside EXPERIENCE by name); Netherlands (Utrecht: 'extra-curricular activities and interests'); FRANCE (Campus France, verbatim, for an applicant short on professional experience: 'you can mention your voluntary work experience, your unpaid jobs or your extracurricular activities' -- which also closes S-017's documented French gap for this one question); Germany (Ehrenamt und Engagement, commercial sources only, but convergent); Ireland (UCC: 'Relevant voluntary experience is of interest. Experience of organising academic-related societies is also useful'); US (NACAC, ~70% of colleges). WHAT IS DESTINATION-DEPENDENT IS THE HEADING, AND IT COMES FROM THE FUNDER OR THE FORMAT, NOT THE COUNTRY. Sweden's SISGP does not mandate 'NETWORK-CIVIL SOCIETY ENGAGEMENT' because Sweden has a norm -- it mandates it because that funder's template does, and R-064 makes altering the category set an eligibility failure. Rhodes calls the same content '2. Volunteering/Community/Leadership' and routes it by PAY, not by subject (R-080), which is why ExperienceEntry.unpaid exists. Two different headings, two funders, one country each -- and neither generalises to the country. CERTIFICATES ARE THE SHARPER CASE: Europass has NO training section, because its education section IS 'EDUCATION AND TRAINING' -- one heading holding 'a bachelor's degree and a professional certification' alike -- and SISGP's mandated category set uses that same name. So on the two variants where this platform has the least freedom, a separate Certificates heading would be WRONG and the content folds into education. Anywhere a format is not imposed, Queensland, Toronto, Berkeley and German guidance all give it a heading of its own. So the rule for this platform is: country decides LAYOUT (S-008's DACH grid, S-018's Nordic minimalism, S-020's Turkiye/Azerbaijan conservatism), the destination decides HEADINGS. Section inventory belongs to cv_format_requirement and funder_template, both of which are already per-programme and per-funder -- never to a country table. (tehsil: one fidelity gap found while checking this. cv_europass.html overrides only `summary` and `languages`, so it inherits cv_base.html's '

Education

' and prints EDUCATION where Europass's own editor prints EDUCATION AND TRAINING. R-053 defines our Europass output as a self-rendered variant matching the editor's sections, so that heading is wrong today -- and it is also the heading a certificates feature would have to fold into. cv_base.html's h2 sits OUTSIDE {% block education_entries %}, so fixing it means moving the heading inside a block, which touches cv_german_tabular.html too.)

Rule: Cambridge's layout rules, read off the 43-page booklet and kept as a block because they are one house style. Verbatim where it matters. TWO CLAUSES WERE ADJUDICATED 2026-09-15 against Harvard Griffin GSAS's academic-CV guide, which is the same genre for the other audience. On ITALICS, Harvard overrules Cambridge: "Avoid text boxes, underlining, and shading; ITALICS MAY BE USED IN MODERATION" -- so on an ACADEMIC CV italics are permitted, Cambridge's blanket avoidance is the employment reading, and tehsil's three uses (a degree's English gloss, a research funder, an award's detail) are moderate and stay. On NOTE FORM, Harvard independently agrees and makes it two universities on two continents: "Use active verbs and SENTENCE FRAGMENTS (NOT FULL SENTENCES) to describe your experiences. Avoid pronouns (e.g. I, me), and minimize articles (a, and, the)." tehsil's bullets are full sentences ending in full stops, so that clause is unmet and the sources now converge on it. (a) "Avoid underlining and italics -- they can make the CV look too fussy and disrupt the flow." S-006 banned underlining only, so the ITALIC half is new -- and tehsil renders `.gloss` in italic for a degree's English translation, a research entry's funder and an award's detail line. It is a UK EMPLOYMENT booklet and S-011 requires italic journal titles in a citation, so this does not bind the citation; it is a live question everywhere else. (b) "Avoid columns and tables. They can look rigid and tend to draw the eye to the lines rather than to the information within them." A READABILITY argument, independent of S-032's machine-parsing one and of S-008's DACH mandate -- three separate reasons now, two against and one for. (c) "Avoid or limit the use of complete sentences on the CV. Note form is usual ('I increased the sales' > 'increased sales')" -- stronger than S-026's active-verb rule, and tehsil's real bullets are full sentences ending in full stops. (d) "Don't use 'Other' in a heading: it either suggests something unimportant ... or it indicates that you don't know how the experience collected in that section is relevant", which rules out Queensland's 'Other experience' heading by name. (e) "Be absolutely consistent and follow the same order within each section, e.g. give the name of employer and then job title, or vice versa, but not a mix." tehsil satisfies this by reading it as what-then-where: degree then institution, role then employer. (f) "Titles and headings don't need full stops; they hold the reader up." (g) "One style of bullet point is enough. Using different bullets or extra indentation for subcategories is likely to add confusion rather than clarity" -- already done, cv_base.html's single `ul` indent. (h) "Avoid splitting sections across pages. Someone skimming will turn the page and start reading from the next heading, so the information carried over from the previous section will get lost." tehsil pins the weaker halves (`.entry{break-inside:avoid}`, `h2{break-after:avoid}`) and CANNOT satisfy the strong one: a four-post Experience section does not fit on one page of a two-page CV. (i) "Eye-tracking research shows that readers tend to skim a page in an 'F' pattern ... place the most important information (keywords) as close to the left side of your page as possible, and avoid the 'dead zone' on the right side." This is S-024's left-loading claim from a university source and WITHOUT the contaminated timing figures S-024 warns about -- and it is the affirmative case for S-007: the date belongs on the right BECAUSE the right is the dead zone.
Scope: universal (UK employment; read across with care)
Source (tier): University of Cambridge Careers Service, 'CVs & Applications for Undergraduate & Masters Students' (2017, 43pp)
Confidence: High (as a house style) / Medium that each clause transfers to graduate admissions

Rule: Three things Cambridge settles that this catalog had left open. (a) THE PERSONAL PROFILE. "Profiles were very trendy for a while, but they are not universally popular. They can be cringeworthy, and many employers prefer to read the facts in the CV, not a subjective summary. In the UK, they are generally unnecessary and best left out." That is a country-scoped verdict on `CVContent.summary`, which tehsil already defaults to null and refuses to write without a confirmed PERSONAL fact -- so the default is right and this is the source for it. It also gives the exceptions: a summary of key skills "can help to give focus", and a profile is warranted where the job itself is writing pithy copy. (b) CV TYPES. Two exist -- chronological and skills-based (organised thematically by competency) -- "In practice, a hybrid of the two types often works well: you present education and employment histories in reverse chronology, and then use skills headings to organise and expand on your relevant achievements." tehsil renders only the chronological form, which S-001 endorses for a master's applicant; the skills-based form is listed with its own negatives ("if you make it hard for an employer to see your 'story', they might worry that you're trying to hide something"). Recorded so nobody builds it by accident. (c) THE CREATIVE CV. "Be very wary of using this option. Even design agencies say that they typically prefer a traditional CV. They would look to your design portfolio for evidence of your creative skills." Corroborates S-015 from the strongest tier yet. Also, on naming: "Create headings and sections on the CV that are meaningful to your prospective employer, e.g. 'publishing experience' or 'administration experience'" -- custom headings are a tailoring lever tehsil does not have, its heading set being fixed.
Source (tier): University of Cambridge Careers Service, 'CVs & Applications for Undergraduate & Masters Students' (2017, 43pp)

Rule: GAPS AND WEAK RESULTS -- and this SUPERSEDES the shape S-041 proposed. Cambridge gives the gap entry's actual wording: "The best approach is usually a simple statement, with a positive slant where appropriate", and every example it prints has NO EMPLOYER at all -- "Glandular fever, now fully recovered"; "Intermitted for health reasons (2 terms)"; "Career break (12 months): travelling in South East Asia"; "Full-time carer for family member"; "Parental leave (6 months)"; "3 months' full-time job-hunting". So S-041 was half right and its fix was wrong: relaxing ExperienceEntry.bullets to min_length=0 would still not represent any of these, because `employer` is required at min_length=1 too. A gap is a DATED STATEMENT, not an employment entry, and it needs its own shape. The same page is explicit that an untrue one is dangerous -- "Your application is part of your contract of employment, and for that reason it must be truthful" -- while warning against "too much honesty: don't dwell on perceived negatives". On WEAK RESULTS: "If you have better subsequent results, then just put those"; "You could specify, alongside your overall grade, papers or options where your results were better"; "Does 'Education' have to be the first section on the CV?"; and decisively, "If you exclude grades completely, the reader will probably assume the worst" -- which is the affirmative source for S-027's 'the grade is expected rather than optional'. One more, for an international applicant: "Avoid Cambridge jargon like Tripos, Part 1A, etc. Use words everyone will understand" -- the general form of R-034, applied to course and stage names rather than to the degree title.
Binding or advisory: advisory; BINDING where a programme requires a gap-free CV (R-011, R-020)

Rule: DOES THE CV DIFFER BY DISCIPLINE? Asked because a science/engineering CV and an arts one plainly look different in the wild. The answer, from the sources rather than from intuition: discipline changes TWO things and neither is the one people reach for. (1) WHICH EXTRA HEADINGS EXIST. Toronto: "Every CV will include information found under standard headings such as education, professional experience, teaching and research experience, publications, academic administrative experience, professional development, and professional memberships. However, there are additional headings that may be DISCIPLINE SPECIFIC." UPenn: "CVs vary slightly from discipline to discipline." (2) THE ORDER OF THE CATEGORIES, and CITATION STYLE AND PUBLICATION ORDERING. Harvard Griffin GSAS is the most explicit and it goes further than the rest: "And most importantly...Follow the conventions of your field! Different academic disciplines have different standards and expectations, ESPECIALLY IN THE ORDER OF CATEGORIES. Check out CVs from recent graduates of your department, and others in your field, to ensure you are following your field's norms." On citation, Toronto: "The manner in which you order and present your publications varies from discipline to discipline and it is important to consult with your department for best practices." That is S-011's 'discipline-enforced' clause, and it is the ONE place discipline genuinely binds. WHAT DOES **NOT** VARY BY DISCIPLINE: layout, typography, length, entry shape, the order of the core sections. Cambridge's 43-page booklet prints twelve worked CVs across computer science, law, philosophy, social sciences, journalism and arts and applies ONE set of layout rules to all of them; what differs between its samples is the heading set, tailored to the TARGET -- 'Project Experience' for the software applicant, 'Public Speaking & Debating Experience' for the would-be barrister, 'Experience of Working for Social Change' for the impact incubator. UCC says the same in one line: "The presence and sequence of headings will vary according [to] the experience of the candidate and the nature of the post." Candidate and post -- not subject. SEARCHED AND NOT FOUND: any university source stating that a MASTER'S ADMISSIONS CV differs by discipline. Everything asserting a STEM-vs-humanities split (publication share, h-index, teaching weight, length) is either commercial or about FACULTY hiring, where the humanities postdoc is often an instructor-of-record and the split is real. Do not carry it back to a two-page admissions CV. (tehsil: the axis we branch on is the TRACK, not the discipline -- render._section_order picks _RESEARCH_SECTIONS when the CV has research to lead with, deciding from the applicant's own content rather than from a subject label, and constraints.resolve_track separately asks what programme is being applied to. That is UCC's 'experience of the candidate and nature of the post' almost exactly, and it is the better axis: an engineer with four supervised posts and two papers needs the research order, and a historian with none does not, whatever their subjects say. THE REAL GAP IS CITATION STYLE: _cv_citation.html renders ONE format for everybody, so the discipline-enforced half of S-011 is unmet. Fixing it is a per-destination or per-discipline citation variant, and it is the only discipline-shaped change this audit found worth making.)

Rule: WHAT THE NON-UK ADMISSIONS OFFICES ACTUALLY DEMAND, and it is far more prescriptive than any careers service. These are ADMISSIONS pages, not advice, so they bind. ETH ZURICH, verbatim: "Please upload an up-to-date, chronological curriculum vitae IN TABLE FORM, leaving nothing out. Begin with your UPPER SECONDARY SCHOOL GRADUATION and include all details right up to the time of application, with exact entries regarding your education (schools attended, studies etc.) and any work experience pertaining to your future plans. LEAVE NO TIME GAPS: also list periods when you did not attend school, study or work (e.g. longer periods of travel or time off)." And separately: "Please write the curriculum vitae in the TEACHING LANGUAGE of the desired degree programme." TUM, whose style guide is quantitative where everyone else is advisory: PDF, A4, "Times New Roman or Arial", "12 point", margins "2 centimeters", line spacing "1.5-fold", "chronological and tabular", periods given with month and year and starting from ELEMENTARY SCHOOL (its own example: "Elementary School Sample City 09/2001 - 09/2005"), first name, surname and DATE OF BIRTH, and "must not contain any gaps longer than 3 months" after leaving school. The EU (Europass) template is explicitly permitted. HARVARD GSD (M.Arch I), verbatim: "Upload a resume or CV that includes full and part-time employment, education, fellowships, extra-curricular university activities, community service, honors, awards, professional registration and societies, publications, avocations, HOBBIES, and travel. If you served in the military, indicate rank on entry and rank on separation. Please provide a complete employment and educational history, INCLUDING INFORMATION ABOUT ANY GAPS. While brevity is valued, please do not feel limited to one page." STANFORD GSE: "There is no page limit, though we typically see resumes of one page with 12-point font and regular, one-inch margins." HARVARD KENNEDY SCHOOL: "it is okay if your resume is several pages long", and it asks for volunteer and public service work, leadership, extracurricular activities and interests. FOUR THINGS THIS SETTLES. (1) The GAP entry is not a style preference -- ETH, TUM, Harvard GSD, DAAD PRIME (R-011) and uni-assist (R-020) all require it, and ETH and TUM require periods of NON-activity to be listed by name. See S-045: tehsil cannot represent one, because ExperienceEntry requires both an employer and a bullet. (2) TABULAR IS NOT ONLY DACH. ETH says table form and TUM says tabular, both for master's ADMISSION, which raises S-008's 'Medium' bindingness: cv_german_tabular.html is the right renderer for Switzerland as well as Germany. (3) SECONDARY SCHOOL IS DESTINATION-DEPENDENT, and the two camps are flatly opposed: ETH wants upper-secondary graduation onward, TUM wants ELEMENTARY school onward, while UCC says "It is typical to omit second-level qualifications" and Lancaster "It isn't necessary to incorporate GCSE's and A'levels". A CV cannot satisfy both, so it is a per-destination variant like every other clash in this catalog. (4) TUM's TYPOGRAPHY DOES NOT MATCH OURS: cv_base.html renders 11pt with line-height 1.3, and TUM requires 12pt at 1.5 -- so a CV rendered today is non-compliant for TUM on two measurable counts, and changing the base would change page count for everyone (see S-004). Per-destination, not global. (A note on hobbies, because the sources look contradictory and are not: Harvard GSD and HKS ASK for hobbies and interests at master's admission, while Lancaster says "Do not include any reference to hobbies/interests" -- for an ACADEMIC JOB CV. That is S-039's audience split again, from a third direction.)
Binding or advisory: BINDING where the admissions page states it
Source (tier): ETH Zurich admissions (eApply Master's summary); Technical University of Munich application style guide; Harvard Graduate School of Design admissions; Stanford Graduate School of Education admissions; Harvard Kennedy School admissions FAQ
Confidence: High (each quoted from the institution's own admissions page)

"Stick to a common font, such as Times New Roman, using a font size of 10 to 12 point" (= S-002). "Margins should be equal on all four sides and be 3/4 to 1 inch in size" (= S-003, exactly). That is Cambridge's 'bucket CV' under another name and it is, structurally, tehsil's VerifiedFact ledger: two university careers services independently prescribe store-everything-then-tailor as the method, which is the architecture this platform already has. Rule: WHAT TO CALL A RESEARCH POSITION -- and why this platform must not answer the question for the applicant. The titles are all real and all attested. Harvard Griffin GSAS's own sample CVs use FIVE of them: "Graduate Researcher", "Research Assistant", "Graduate Research Assistant", "Research Assistant I" and "Undergraduate Research Assistant". UConn's undergraduate-research CV guidance lists "Research Assistant, Independent Researcher, Laboratory Technician" and treats "Research Assistant", "Research Intern" and "Undergraduate Research Project" as equally acceptable headings. The rough division of usage: RESEARCH ASSISTANT for a post held under faculty supervision (the commonest, and appointed at graduate level more often than not); RESEARCH INTERN where the post was time-limited, a summer or a semester; UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCHER or UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH ASSISTANT where the status itself needs stating. UConn's framing of what matters is the operative one -- "The order of information may vary ... Regardless of the order, it is essential that you are CONSISTENT" -- and the general CV rule is that a title may be CLARIFIED but not upgraded, since a reference or a background check contradicts an invented one. (tehsil: THE TITLE IS NOT OURS TO CHOOSE, and the architecture already enforces that rather than merely discouraging it. `title` is half of the EXPERIENCE spec's IDENTITY in apps/documents/verification.py -- `identity=("employer", "title")` -- which is the strictest class of claim there is. A generated CV that renamed a 'Research Intern' to 'Research Assistant' would match NO fact in the ledger, come back UNSUPPORTED, and block the draft. That is correct: the title is a claim about what an institution appointed the student as, and this platform verifies claims against a document rather than improving them. If a title is genuinely unclear to a foreign reader, the sanctioned routes are the ones that already exist -- a gap question to the student, or the counsellor's own edit -- never a silent rewrite at generation.)
Source (tier): Harvard Griffin GSAS 'CVs and Cover Letters' (2025) sample CVs; University of Connecticut Office of Undergraduate Research, CV and Resume guidance

Rule: QUESTIONS A COUNSELLOR ASKS THAT NO RULE HERE ASKED FOR -- found 2026-09-16 by auditing the counsellor-review design against the catalog and then searching for what the catalog itself lacked. Nine items, ranked. (1) MEDIUM OF INSTRUCTION of the prior degree. Many destinations waive IELTS/TOEFL where the bachelor's was taught in English -- USC, Cornell ("medium of instruction indicated on the transcript or easily verified on the institution's website"), Boston University ("the transcript must clearly state that English is the sole language of instruction"), and Arizona State has a formal 'English Proficiency Exemption Form: Medium of Instruction (MOI)'. Australia Awards' mandated template already asks for MEDIUM OF INSTRUCTION per degree (R-065). The waiver is almost never offered unprompted: the applicant has to ask and supply a certificate. AND IT IS NOT UNIVERSAL -- owner correction 2026-09-16: the conditions differ by destination. USC waives only where English is BOTH the language of instruction AND the country's only official language; Cornell requires English to be an official language of the COUNTRY as well; Boston University requires the transcript to state English as the SOLE language of instruction. A degree taught in English in Azerbaijan or Germany earns a waiver at some destinations and none at others. So the STANDARD layer gathers the fact -- medium of instruction, and whether the university certifies it -- and never promises anything; whether that fact earns an exemption is a per-destination rule that the programme layer fetches and applies on top (S-042's principle, again). The catalog had the field concept in one funder rule and no schema field and no question. Highest value of the nine because it is the one fact that can remove a whole requirement -- at the destinations that accept it. (2) EXCHANGE / MOBILITY SEMESTERS, UNCOMPLETED PROGRAMMES, DOUBLE DEGREES. ETH Zurich, verbatim: transcripts "from every university attended, including any mobility or exchange programmes and study programmes which were not completed; double-degree programmes require transcripts from both universities" -- and its CV must be consistent with that ("leaving nothing out", S-047). An Erasmus semester is an EducationEntry the student never thinks to list; an abandoned programme is one they think to hide, and ETH treats the omission as the fault. Three questions, one moment. (3) POSITIONS OF RESPONSIBILITY, STUDENT COMMITTEES, ASSOCIATIONS. Toronto Mississauga's CV checklist asks it outright -- "Am I a member of any associations or student clubs relevant to my field of study?" -- and lists "Academic committees served on (name of committee, your role, dates)" and "Student organizations involved in (name of organization, your role, dates)". Cambridge names the heading 'Positions of responsibility'; Harvard Kennedy School asks for 'Leadership experiences'. S-039 rejected MEMBERSHIPS as a SECTION for a master's applicant; that stands. As a QUESTION it is one line and the answer feeds the community/leadership content Oxford, SISGP and Harvard GSD all want. (4) THE DESTINATION COUNTRY'S LANGUAGE. DAAD asks German-capable applicants for a 'DAAD language evaluation form signed by a faculty member of the German Department'; R-041 wants CEFR for European contexts. Pack-gated: a pack containing German programmes prompts "What is your German level?" -- a fact the CV omits because the student did not know it mattered. (5) PERSONAL OR OPEN-SOURCE PROJECTS WITH A PUBLIC REPOSITORY. Cambridge's own computer-science sample gives 'Project Experience' its own heading; R-026 names Projects in the taught order; S-013 wants GitHub in the header. For a STEM applicant the repository IS the evidence. Field-gated at pack time. (6) ECTS CREDITS. R-038 has required them for European programmes since the first research pass; `ects_credits` exists on EducationEntry; nothing asks. Region-gated. (7) THESIS GRADE where graded separately from the degree (German, Dutch and Nordic systems do). Ask ONLY when the degree is COMPLETE (end_date in the past) and a thesis_title exists -- owner correction 2026-09-16: a fourth-year applicant has not received a thesis grade, and asking for one is the wrong question. The same condition governs the DEGREE grade: an in-progress degree has a grade so far or an expected classification, not a final mark -- Cambridge's own worked sample prints 'Second Year, 2.1 expected' -- and the existing missing_grade detector asked every degree 'What grade did you finish with?', which was wrong for the real CV's in-progress MSc. (8) TALK OR POSTER for each presentation -- Toronto Mississauga: "Consider distinguishing between oral and poster presentations". Low. (9) OUTREACH / SCIENCE-COMMUNICATION WRITING -- Toronto's main guide files 'media articles, blogs and book chapters' under publications with their own sub-heading. Low for a master's applicant. SEARCHED AND NOT ASKABLE, recorded so nobody re-derives them: GRE/GMAT (no university source puts it on the CV -- it travels on the application form; the only advice to list it is commercial); DRIVING LICENCE (a Europass employment field, irrelevant to admission; the current editor's optional-section list could not be read from europass.europa.eu because the editor is a script, so this rests on the field's existence in the 2020 redesign rather than on a verbatim); PATENTS and PROFESSIONAL REGISTRATION (Harvard GSD asks for the latter; both rare at master's level -- fold into the wording of the certificates and publications questions rather than ask separately).
Binding or advisory: advisory; (1) and (2) BINDING where the destination states them (ETH, Australia Awards)
